extracted.intended_audience: educated travellers and readers of religious and architectural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for readers and travellers on how to interpret and appreciate Gothic cathedrals—their structure, art, and liturgical meaning—and on assessing the cultural and spiritual influence of the Bible. Includes practical viewing advice, structural and material criteria, and interpretive lenses connecting art, theology, and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority over literal translation
rubrics_metrics.description: The gist of the Bible's influence lies not merely in translating Hebrew and Greek into a common language, but in their presentation to the Church as of common authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise how establishing the Scriptures as a common authoritative body (rather than just easier language) shaped their effect; historical controversies (e.g., Gentile Christians doubting Jewish law observance) illustrate that authority and communal reception matter more than literal linguistic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess influence by sincere reception and obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: When measuring the Bible's power, examine the persons who receive the Word with joy and obey it in truth rather than those who accept parts and refuse others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude factional or enthusiast readers whose partial devotion or zeal produces distorted outcomes; the history of the Church should be studied via the faithful reception rather than contentious debates or corrupt readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold framework for judging Christianity's hold
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine Christianity's hold under three heads: (1) the power of the Cross and theory of salvation on the heart; (2) the operation of the Jewish and Greek Scriptures on the intellect; (3) the influence on morals of the living hierarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinct dimensions when comparing men as they are and as they might have been; ask specific counterfactuals (e.g., what would Europe be without charity/labour, without Biblical literature, or without its hierarchy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for authentic Christian effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The pure word of God is recognised only when the Cross is received with courage, the Scripture searched with honesty, and the Pastor heard in faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this tripod of conditions as a test for authenticity; beware modern reversals that transform self-denial into comfort or commerce—such reversals undermine genuine Christian influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of general inspiration (not limited to elite authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspiration should be attributed to the whole body of believers to the degree they partake of grace, not restricted to particular persons or words; inspiration varies with trust and obedience (a child inspired as a child, a maiden as a maiden).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rigid distinctions (inspiration of words vs acts) and resist assigning infallible truth to human linguistic forms; measure inspiration experimentally by lived obedience and reception rather than doctrinal assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit claims of special dictation and infallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Special calls or dictation are only ascribed in certain passages for particular needs; one cannot attach infallible truth to any form of human language in which these have been delivered to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat exceptional passages as limited phenomena; preserve humility about the fallibility of human expression even in sacred texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psalter as practical guide for personal and social wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: The Psalter functioned as the service book of the Church and, in its first half, contains the sum of personal and social wisdom—specific psalms (1, 8, 12, 14, 15, 19, 23, 24; 48, 72, 75; 104) serve for personal guidance, righteous government, and anticipation of natural science respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage learning and believing key psalms as practical moral and civic instruction; treat the Psalter as a compendium of everyday spiritual resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess scope by cataloguing biblical literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the Bible's breadth by its composite contents: I. Fall/Flood stories; II. Patriarchs; III. Moses and moral law; IV. Kings/Proverbs/Ecclesiasticus; V. Prophets; VI. The story of Christ; VII. St. John's moral law and Apocalypse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this table-of-contents approach to show the Bible's unmatched range and to compare what other literatures might have supplied in its absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic builder's purpose: height, spaciousness, economy, security
rubrics_metrics.description: A good Gothic builder aimed to raise an edifice as high and as spacious as possible with calculable and visible security, in no protracted time, and without oppressive human labour or exhausting a city's resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Gothic buildings by their structural prudence: ambition balanced by local means, efficient construction schedules, and avoidance of civic overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material honesty and quarry practice
rubrics_metrics.description: French medieval builders used stones as they lay in the bed (thick beds used full thickness, thin beds used thin stones), never sawing the natural blocks, thus conserving the stone's natural strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess masonry by whether it preserves the stone's grain and natural strength; note the historical practice (and its geographic persistence) as a criterion of authentic construction technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural aims: light, intelligibility, and restrained ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: The builder's objective was to admit as much light as was consistent with comfort; to make the structure intelligibly admirable not curious or confusing; to enrich the structure with ornament sufficient for beauty yet not ostentatious; and to make exterior sculpture an alphabet and epitome of the religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a cathedral, look for balance between illumination and comfort, clarity of structural logic, tasteful restraint in decoration, and didactic sculptural programs that teach the faithful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liturgical program determines plan (choir centrality and chapels)
rubrics_metrics.description: The choir functioned as the part where Divine presence was constant (akin to the Jewish Holy of Holies); aisles and transepts served more public functions, while radiating eastern chapels each dedicated to a saint informed the apse's disposition and supporting buttresses/piers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the building's liturgical logic—only by sympathy with the spiritual imagination that produced the plan can one properly delight in its form; read architecture as enacted worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the cathedral as literal 'House of God' and social organism
rubrics_metrics.description: Every part of old Christian architecture is literal: the cathedral is the House of God, surrounded by lodgings for servants, and carvings and furnishings are designed to serve both divine and human needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid purely symbolic or detached aesthetic readings; interpret carvings, seating, and spatial arrangements in light of their practical and devotional functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate craftsmanship and constructional detail (wood-carving and stalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the choir stalls and wood-carving for material quality (trained oak), finesse of carving (canopy crowning canopy, filigree leafage), joinery (morticed joints, no nails), and compositional unity across masters and apprentices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to technical details (wood provenance, wages, contracts, dates, master/apprentice roles) and to the visual effect: morticed joinery, bas-reliefs, and integrated design—these are central to the work's lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical production context to appreciate the work
rubrics_metrics.description: The accounts of contracts, wages, duration (e.g., fourteen years for Amiens stalls), and the collaboration of masters, apprentices, image-cutters, and supervising canons are integral to understanding and valuing the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquire into patronage, contracts, material sources, and project organization—knowing these facts deepens aesthetic appreciation and explains choices of subject, placement, and workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended visitor approaches and viewing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: If time allows, approach from the chalk hill to view the cathedral in relation to town and height; if pressed for time, enter via the south transept and give priority to the choir—if you have only a quarter of an hour, devote it wholly to the choir.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan your route according to weather and time: a long, winding approach through old streets aids appreciation; a short visit should focus on the choir and key views; small preparations (a cheerful temper, bonbons for children) help set the mood.
